processing: Coarse shoots with stems are bound into brush-shaped bundles with thread, then baked repeatedly at low temperature, with cooling and rehydration between rounds. Character falls between a baked green and an oolong.
harvest_season: After Grain Rain, picked mature at one bud with three or four leaves, stems included.
appearance_dry: Stout straight dark-green strands bound with coloured thread into a brush-like bundle.
appearance_wet: Long mature leaves with stems, which loosen from the bundle as it steeps.
taste_profile: Mellow and full with an oolong-like aroma, sometimes floral, and very durable over repeated steeps.

brewing.notes: These are general oolong settings. Use one bundle per pot and let it open in hot water; the tea holds up well to many steeps.

vintage_note: Recent revivals were started by orders, and little is documented about regular yearly production, so ask for the production year. A Guizhou relative is kept for about two years before drinking, as it is harsh when new.
description:
Longxu Cha, dragon whisker tea, is a bundled tea: long leaves tied with thread into something like a brush head. The usual account puts its home in the Wuyi Mountains and Jian'ou in northern Fujian, and its other name, Shu Cha, simply means bundled tea.

Picking is late, after Grain Rain, with mature leaf and stem. The binding is the distinctive part, while baking is the hard part: many gentle low-temperature rounds with rests in between, so moisture can work out from the core of the bundle. Jian'ou makers have moved to bamboo fibre from silk thread for hygiene.

A Shuixian-based version gives an orange-yellow liquor, mellow and very durable, with an oolong-like aroma. Drop in a whole bundle, use hot water, and do not expect it to open in the first steep.

The name is not unique. A Guizhou tea with similar bundles, called Zhuangyuan Bi, is made mainly as green and yellow tea and is aged about two years, and the same word turns up as a folk name for vine tea, a different plant altogether. Some listings also place it elsewhere, including Jiangxi and Sichuan, so ask what the leaf and origin really are. Thread colours can mark use: yellow for temples, red for weddings, blue for funerals.
history:
The oldest usual citation is Lu Tiancan's Qing work Xu Cha Jing, which lists longxu among the names of Wuyi riverside teas. Whether that name meant today's bundled tea is an inference by later tea people, not a settled fact. In Guizhou, its 19th-century relative is said to have come from Yanshan in Jiangxi.

The tea was largely forgotten until the reform era. Tea expert Ye Xingwei made a few batches in Wuyi and Jian'ou in the early 1980s for Anxi merchants, and around 2004 Zu Gengrong, former head of the Wuyi Mountain tea farm, resumed making it after orders from Malaysia and other Southeast Asian buyers.
